We'll start this chapter by revisiting the idea of radioactive spider bites affecting reaction times. This time, though, we'll move beyond one unusually quick kid and consider a whole sample of Spider-People. That will present a problem that we'll solve using the tools we've picked up over the last few chapters: $z$-scores, probability, sampling distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem. By putting them together, we'll complete our first hypothesis test.

## Spider-Man revisited

Back in Chapter 5 we considered the possibility that a radioactive spider bite might have improved the reaction times of one individual. We supposed that following the bite, our test subject,Peter Parker, had a reaction time of 189 milliseconds on a test for which the general population had a mean of 284 milliseconds and a standard deviation of 50 milliseconds. We calculated his $z$-score to be $-1.9$. Assuming reaction times form a normal distribution, the probability of seeing a score this fast or faster is less than three percent.

In other words, we asked what we would expect if the spider bite had done nothing and Peter's reaction time still came from the population of unbitten kids. We would only see a score this fast or faster about three times out of a hundred. That didn't prove that the spider bite had changed his reaction time. But his score was unusual under the no-change explanation, which gave us some reason to doubt it.

That calculation already contained the basic logic of a hypothesis test: if the spider bite had done nothing, what were the chances of seeing a reaction time this fast or faster?

Still, it isn't entirely obvious that being bitten by a radioactive spider ought to *improve* your reaction time. It might slow you down, or merely give you a nasty bite. For now, let's remain open to a change in either direction. We'll return to why that matters when we distinguish one-tailed and two-tailed tests.

But real research doesn't usually rely on examining just one individual. We usually want a *sample*---a bunch of kids who we treated to radioactive spider bites to see if it would alter their reaction times. Obviously in the real world this experiment probably would not make it past the ethics board, but the Spiderverse™️ provides just such a scenario.

![A sample of my son's toy Spider-People, $n = 3$](resources/figures/3-spidermen.gif){#fig-spidermen}

So say we have a sample of three kids, all bitten by radioactive spiders, and we measure their reaction times. The *sample mean* is 189 milliseconds, the same as Peter Parker's individual score. But now we have a sample of three people, not just one. How does that change our analysis? Is it just as surprising as a single score of 189 ms? More surprising? Less? Surprising *enough* to count as evidence that the population mean changed?

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-spider-sample-reflection.qmd >}}

### From the example to the terminology

The move from one Spider-Man to a sample of Spider-People changes the calculation, but not the general logic. For Peter's individual score, we used the population distribution to ask what reaction times we would commonly see if nothing had changed. For our sample mean, we'll need the sampling distribution to ask what sample means we would commonly see under that same no-change assumption.

Let's attach the main terms to that logic now. The spider bite is the *treatment*: the condition or intervention applied to our sample. A change in reaction times associated with the treatment would be a *treatment effect*, though a significance test alone cannot establish what caused the change. We observe only one treated sample, but we care about the hypothetical population it represents---what would happen if everyone received the treatment. The sample mean is our clue to that population mean.

The formal procedure we're about to use is called *Null Hypothesis Significance Testing*, or *NHST*. We begin with a skeptical working model: suppose the spider bites did nothing, so the population of bitten kids still has the same mean reaction time as the population of unbitten kids, 284 milliseconds. This is the *null hypothesis*, $H_0$. The *alternative hypothesis*, $H_1$, says that the population mean changed:

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$$

If the null is true, our three Spider-People should behave like a random sample from a population with a mean of 284. We can work out what sorts of sample means that population would commonly produce, then see where our observed mean of 189 falls.

{{< interactive-figure zTestInferentialDiagram makeInferentialDiagram options='{"preset":"z-test"}' fallback="Inferential process diagram for a z test." >}}

But here's the rub. Sample means vary due to sampling error, even when the population mean hasn't changed. So if our treated sample has a different mean, we need to judge whether the difference is more than we would commonly expect from sampling error alone. We do that by imagining the sampling distribution we would get if the treatment had no effect, then asking how common or uncommon our observed sample mean would be in that distribution.

And that raises another question: how unlikely is unlikely enough? Before analyzing the data, we choose a *decision criterion*, called *alpha* and written $\alpha$. If we choose the conventional $\alpha = .05$, we're deciding that results in the most extreme five percent of the null distribution will count as sufficiently unusual to reject the null. We'll return to the details shortly. First, let's work out how unusual our sample mean actually is.

## From individual scores to sample means {#sec-spider-test}

We have all the tools we need. First, let's put the calculation for Peter Parker's single score in front of us again. We plug his reaction time of 189 milliseconds into the individual-score equation and get $-1.9$.

$$ z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{189 - 284}{50} = -1.9 $$

We can look up $z = 1.9$ in the unit normal table to find the lower-tail probability: $P(z \le -1.9) = .0287$. So if Peter Parker's reaction time really came from the population of unbitten kids, we would see a score this fast or faster about three times out of a hundred. This is the directional question we asked in Chapter 5, not yet a formal two-tailed test.

{{< interactive-figure peterZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":1.86,"to":1.94,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":1.9,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 1.86 to 1.94, with the area to the right of z = 1.90, .0287, highlighted." >}}

For the sample of three, we locate the sample mean among all the sample means that the population could produce. The equations from Chapter 7 tell us that this sampling distribution has the same mean as the population and a standard error of $\sigma_M = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$. The Central Limit Theorem tells us about its shape: if the population is normal, the sampling distribution is normal at any sample size; otherwise, it becomes approximately normal as the sample size increases. Because our sample contains only three observations, this calculation relies on our simplifying assumption that reaction times are normally distributed.

The test we're using is called a *one-sample $z$-test*. It tests a hypothesized population mean, written $\mu_0$, when the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is treated as known and the sampling distribution of the mean is normal or sufficiently close to normal. Its test statistic is:

$$z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$$

This test isn't used very often because in real research we rarely know the population standard deviation. Usually we have to estimate it from sample data, which is why we'll need the $t$-test later. But the $z$-test is a good place to start.

For our Spider-People, $\mu_0 = 284$. The Human Benchmark results page supplied that mean; as we admitted in Chapter 5, we invented the population standard deviation of 50 milliseconds for this example. The numerator is therefore the same difference we calculated for Peter alone. It's the denominator that changes: we divide by the standard error of the mean rather than the standard deviation of individual scores.

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-sample-z-score.qmd >}}

Putting the values into the equation gives us a $z$-score of $-3.29$:

$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{189 - 284}{50 / \sqrt{3}} = -3.29 $$

That's quite a bit lower than $-1.9$ because sample means vary less than individual scores. A sample mean as far from the population mean as this is less common than an individual score that far away.

And if we look up that $z$-score in the unit normal table, we get a much smaller lower-tail probability: $P(z \le -3.29) = .0005$.

{{< interactive-figure spidermenZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":3.25,"to":3.33,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":3.29,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 3.25 to 3.33, with the area to the right of z = 3.29, .0005, highlighted." >}}

To show this another way, here's what the sampling distribution looks like and where our sample mean lies in that distribution. Here it's shown in the original units; we could relabel the axis with $z$-scores instead. Remember, the $z$-scores are just a change of label. They don't transform the positions or the variability of the scores. So with the original units, our sample mean is still exactly as far down in that extreme tail of the distribution.

{{< interactive-figure spidermenSamplingDistribution makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"normal","mean":284,"sd":28.87,"xDomain":[165,375],"xTicks":8,"style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"shade":{"to":189},"markers":{"at":189,"label":"M = 189","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},"animate":true,"labels":{"x":"Sample mean reaction time (ms), n = 3"}}' fallback="Sampling distribution of mean reaction times for samples of three, centered on 284 ms with standard error 28.87 ms; a vertical line marks the sample mean of 189 ms far down in the lower tail." >}}

In other words, if spider bites leave the population mean at 284 milliseconds, getting a sample of three people with an average of 189 milliseconds is vanishingly unlikely. The observed sample is difficult to reconcile with our starting assumption that the bites did nothing. That doesn't prove what caused the difference, but it gives us evidence against the no-change model.

## Formalizing the hypothesis test

We've effectively just completed our first hypothesis test. We used the null as a working model, calculated what it predicted, and found that our sample mean was very difficult to reconcile with it.

Ronald A. Fisher was a British statistician and geneticist, and one of the central figures in the development of modern statistics. Among many other contributions, he helped develop and popularize significance testing and the use of null hypotheses in experimental research. In his 1935 book *The Design of Experiments*, he put the logic rather neatly:

> “Every experiment may be said to exist only in order to give the facts a chance of disproving the null hypothesis.”
>
> ---R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments* [@fisher1935design, p. 16]

“Disproving” is stronger language than we'll usually use. A statistical result cannot establish with logical certainty that the null hypothesis is false. But Fisher's line captures the direction of the argument. We work out what the null hypothesis predicts, then give the data a chance to contradict it. That doesn't mean we begin by believing that the null hypothesis is true. It gives us a precise model to test. We used our knowledge of sampling distributions and probability to determine what kind of sample means would be common or uncommon if the population mean remained unchanged. Then we compared the $z$-score for our Spider-People's sample mean with that null distribution. The observed result was unusually far out in the tail, so it counted as evidence against the null hypothesis.

## The four-step hypothesis testing procedure

We can organize the reasoning we just followed into four steps: state the hypotheses, set the decision criteria, collect and analyze the data, and make a decision.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

We have already stated the hypotheses for our Spider-People. The null says that the population mean reaction time remains 284 milliseconds after a bite. The alternative says that the mean changes:

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$$

Notice that the two hypotheses don't play symmetrical roles in this test. The null gives us a specific population mean: 284 milliseconds. Along with our other assumptions, that value defines a specific sampling distribution. It therefore gives us something we can test directly: if the population mean really is 284, how often would we get a sample mean this far from it or farther?

The alternative hypothesis is less specific. It says that the mean is *not* 284, but that could mean 283, 250, 400, or any other value. It doesn't supply one alternative mean from which we could construct one alternative sampling distribution. So, in the significance test we're doing here, it is the null hypothesis that we test directly. The alternative tells us what counts as a departure from it---in this case, a difference in either direction.

That point can be overstated. We *could* specify a particular alternative, such as $\mu_{\text{bitten}} = 250$. That would give us another sampling distribution to work with, and we'll need just such a specific alternative when we discuss statistical power in the next chapter. But our alternative here, $\mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$, does not make one precise numerical prediction.

The null doesn't have to say that two populations are identical in every imaginable respect. It makes a claim about the particular parameter we're testing---the population mean, in this case. In other statistical tests, the null might state that two treatment conditions have equal population means, or that there is no association between two variables. In broad terms, the null says that the particular effect or relationship we're testing is absent.

These two propositions are logical complements: the bitten population mean is either equal to 284 or it isn't. They can't both be true. But that doesn't make the evidence perfectly symmetrical. We're going to ask how well our data fit the null model. A result that would be very unusual under that model gives us reason to reject it, though it doesn't prove any particular alternative or establish what caused the difference. And a result that isn't unusual under the null only means that we fail to reject it; it doesn't prove the null hypothesis true. The test won't reveal either proposition to be true or false with certainty, but it can tell us whether the data provide sufficient evidence to reject the null.

Hypotheses don't have to concern a treatment. Say we're interested in whether there is an association between the number of years of education someone has completed and their lifetime earnings. The null would say that there is no association between education and income. The alternative would say that there is.

- General research question: Is there an association between education and income? 🎓🤑
    - $H_0$: There is no association between education and income.
    - $H_1$: There is an association between education and income.

If you really think about it, this should be by far the most important and effortful step of the entire research process. Formulating new, interesting, sensible, plausible, meaningful hypotheses isn't easy. Even to begin to come up with reasonable and potentially insightful hypotheses requires familiarity with the existing research and theoretical perspectives on the phenomena you're interested in, a coherent definition of the construct(s) in question and a good sense of what makes for a good operational definition. We won't say much more about *formulating* hypotheses for this class. We'll focus more on what happens next: the statistical analysis used to test them.

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-stating-hypotheses.qmd >}}

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

For step two, we're essentially asking, "if the null hypothesis is true, what sample statistics are we most likely or unlikely to see?" Our statistical model tells us what the null sampling distribution will look like. Exactly how we determine its characteristics depends on the nature of our data and the appropriate test statistic. We'll talk more about that as we go. But in a general sense, we are using our knowledge of probability and sampling to determine what results would be highly unusual under the null hypothesis. If we see one that is sufficiently unusual, we will reject the null.

Here, we need to introduce the terminology of $\alpha$ and $p$-values. The Greek symbol, lowercase $\alpha$, is our decision criterion: a cutoff chosen before we analyze the data. The $p$-value is calculated from the observed data. It is the probability, assuming the null model and its other assumptions are correct, of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one we observed. What counts as "extreme" depends on whether our alternative hypothesis is one- or two-tailed.

By convention, psychology often uses an alpha level of .05, placing the most extreme five percent of the null distribution in the rejection region. If our sample's $p$-value is less than $\alpha$, we call the result statistically significant and reject the null hypothesis. So when you see $p < .05$ in a published journal article, this is what it means. Neither number is the probability that the null hypothesis is true. When the null is true and the test's assumptions hold, $\alpha$ is the long-run probability that the procedure will reject it by mistake.

Why five percent? There is nothing mathematically special about it. Ronald Fisher called it a convenient boundary in an influential 1925 statistics book, building on an older rule of thumb that results about two standard deviations from expectation were noteworthy [@fisher1925statistical, pp. 47--48]. The convention stuck, though other thresholds can be more appropriate when the consequences of a false alarm differ.

The **critical region** contains the sample statistics that would lead us to reject the null hypothesis. Its boundary is the **critical value**. For an upper-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$, for example, the critical value is the 95th percentile of the null distribution: 95 percent lies below it, and five percent lies above it.

### One-tailed and two-tailed tests

We don't have to have just one critical region. If we do, it's called a one-tailed test, because our critical region is in one tail of the distribution. But we can have a two-tailed test where we specify critical regions at both extremes. If we do this, we're dividing our chosen $\alpha$ into two. If $\alpha$ is .05, or five percent, then by having a two-tailed hypothesis test, we're dividing that five percent between the two tails of the distribution, giving two and a half percent at each end that will cause us to reject the null hypothesis.

In percentile terms, the two critical values are at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The middle 95 percent of the null hypothesis distribution lies between them, leaving the most extreme five percent outside them.

Whether we want a one- or two-tailed test depends on how we stated our hypotheses in step one. We talk about directional or non-directional hypotheses. With a one-tailed or directional hypothesis, the researcher specifies in advance that they are looking for either an increase or a decrease. With a two-tailed, non-directional test, we're looking for a difference in either direction. Since we don't really know what radioactive spider bites ought to do to a person's reaction time, our formal Spider-People test will be two-tailed. The main point of step two is that we determine up front what kind of results would lead us to reject the null. We don't choose a convenient tail after seeing the data.

::::: {#act-alpha-critical-regions .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}
## Explore alpha and critical regions

{{< interactive-figure alphaTutorial makeAlphaTutorial fallback="Explore alpha and critical regions. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Two tails" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
The curve shows the sampling distribution of $z$ when the null hypothesis is true. With $\alpha = .05$ split between two tails, the critical values are about $-1.96$ and $1.96$. The shaded regions together contain five percent of the area. Our hypothetical sample has $z = -1.8$, so it falls just short of the lower critical region.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A stricter cutoff" data-action='{"alpha":0.01,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
Reduce alpha to $.01$. The critical regions shrink, and their boundaries move farther from zero, to about $\pm 2.58$. We now require a more extreme result to reject the null. Notice what hasn't changed: the observed $z$ and its $p$-value. Changing our decision criterion doesn't change the evidence in the sample.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A lower tail" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"left","z":-1.8}'}
Now compare a plan that put all of $\alpha = .05$ in the lower tail. Its critical value is about $-1.64$, so $z = -1.8$ would lead us to reject the null. A lower-tailed test is relevant when the prespecified alternative predicts a decrease, such as faster reaction times. We're comparing possible plans here; we don't choose the direction after seeing the result.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="An upper tail" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"right","z":-1.8}'}
An upper-tailed plan puts the same five percent at the other end. Our negative $z$ doesn't support that alternative, and its upper-tailed $p$-value is large. The direction determines which results count as evidence against the null. It changes both the critical region and the calculation of $p$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Try it" data-action='{"controls-open":true,"alpha":0.05,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
Try changing alpha while keeping the observed $z$ fixed. Then move $z$ across a critical boundary. Crossing into the shaded region and getting $p < \alpha$ are two ways of reaching the same decision. When the null is true and the test's assumptions hold, alpha is also the long-run probability of rejecting it by mistake. It isn't the probability that this particular conclusion is wrong.
:::

::::
:::::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to conduct the research, gather data, and calculate the appropriate sample statistics. For our purposes, recall that the version of the Central Limit Theorem we're using assumes independent observations drawn from the same population distribution. Random sampling is one way to support those assumptions, though in practice social scientists often collect data in less tidy ways.

The exact statistic we calculate depends on the nature of the data. We'll encounter several others later, including the $t$-test, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and correlation and regression. They all rely on the same fundamental hypothesis-testing ideas we're outlining here.

### Step 4: Make a decision

And now everything is in place for us to make our decision. If the test statistic falls in the critical region---equivalently, if $p < \alpha$---we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we *fail to reject* it. Failing to reject the null isn't the same as accepting it or showing that nothing happened. It means this study did not provide sufficient evidence against it.

For our two-tailed Spider-People test, $\alpha = .05$ gives critical values of $\pm 1.96$. Our $z$ of $-3.29$ falls in the lower critical region. Counting results at least this far from the null mean in either direction gives $p \approx .0010$. Since $p < \alpha$, we reject the null and call the result statistically significant. The sample would be extraordinarily unusual if the population mean really remained 284 milliseconds. That gives us evidence that the mean changed. It does not, by itself, prove that the spider bites caused the change.

## Practice: CBT for OCD

We'll end by having you perform your own hypothesis test. We're going back to the cognitive behavioral therapy example from Chapter 5, based on a study using the Dimensional Obsessive-Compulsive Scale to measure symptoms before and after treatment [@abramowitz2010docs].

And we're going to play the same slightly dishonest teaching trick again. For the moment, pretend that untreated people with OCD form a known reference population with a mean of 30.25 and a standard deviation of 14.89. A treated sample of 40 people has a mean of 15.49. First articulate the null and alternative hypotheses, then set your decision criteria, calculate the test statistic, and make your decision.


{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-learning-check.qmd >}}

I should tell you that, like when I first used this example in Chapter 5, I'm misusing the data here again. As before, the numbers are from the real study, but 30.25 and 14.89 were pre-treatment *sample statistics*, not known population parameters. More importantly, the mean of 15.49 came from the *same 40 people* measured after treatment. That makes this a related-samples design, so this $z$-test is not the analysis we would use for the real study. We'll return to the actual design, and the test it calls for, when we introduce the related-samples $t$-test in Chapter 13.

## What the test tells us---and what it leaves open

NHST gives us a disciplined way to ask whether a sample result is difficult to explain under a null model. But a statistically significant result needn't be a large or important effect. And a nonsignificant result needn't mean that there is no effect. To understand those possibilities, we need to look more closely at effect size, inferential errors, and statistical power. That's where we'll go next.
